lines: Notice that the first worker did everything right, by its own lights.
It held a lock, it paused for reasons entirely outside its control, and it checked that the lock was still good before resuming.
Everything it could see told it to go ahead. What it couldn't see is the part that matters.
Before choosing, think about what actually stops an arbitrarily long pause from landing wherever it wants.
Nothing you add on the client's own side has a way to guarantee that. Whatever fixes this has to live somewhere the pause can't reach.
answer: Only the storage layer refusing the stale write actually works.
A longer lease just buys more time before the identical failure. Another check just gives the pause one more gap to land in.
The fix has to sit at the one place the pause can't interfere with: the moment the write actually arrives.

lines: Watch what a lease is actually buying here, and what it's costing to buy it.
While it holds, nothing else in the system can possibly be the leader, so a local answer is as good as asking everyone.
That certainty rests entirely on clocks agreeing closely enough. Loosen that assumption and the certainty goes with it.
Pay attention to where exactly the danger lives, because it's not where it looks like it lives.
It's not in the length of the pause. It's in the fact that a pause can start at literally any instant, including the one between your check and your write.
Move the check right up against the write, and you haven't closed that gap. You've just given it a new address.
Notice who's doing the checking now, because that's the entire fix.
Not the client, checking itself. The resource, checking the number arriving with the write against the highest one it's already seen.
A pause can corrupt what a client believes. It can't touch what the resource has already recorded.
Separate what's genuinely different across these four systems from what's identical underneath.
A sequencer, an epoch, a zxid, a term. Four names, four slightly different formats.
Every one of them is a number that only grows, checked by something that refuses to let it go backward.
Think carefully about what a lock can and can't promise, separate from how carefully it's used.
It can promise to coordinate clients who check it and respect what it says. It cannot promise anything about a client who's stopped running entirely.
That's not a flaw in any particular lock. It's a limit on what a lock, by itself, is.
Carry forward the shape of the whole fix, not four separate production names.
A lease buys a local answer, paid for in a clock assumption. No amount of client-side checking survives an unbounded pause. A number that only grows, checked by the thing being written to, does.
Everything else in this topic is that one idea, dressed differently.
Before answering, think about what the storage layer is actually comparing when it rejects a stale write.
It needs to look at a number and know, just from the number, whether something larger has already come through.
answer: A random token tells the storage this write is different from the last one, but nothing about whether it's older or newer.
Without an order to compare against, the storage has no way to pick out the stale write at all.
